Dear Jasleen Ma'am,
It's been a year since I finished my apprenticeship in your carpentry workshop, and I have a confession. For my first six months at the new job, I talked exactly like you. "Measure twice, cut once, beta." "The wood tells you where it wants to split." I even called my apprentice "beta", and he's older than me! Your phrases made me feel like I knew what I was doing when I didn't yet.
Lately I've noticed some of them don't sound like me. I don't say "beta". I explain things with drawings, not proverbs. But "measure twice" stays forever. It's the best advice anyone ever gave me.
So thank you for lending me your voice until I found mine.
With respect,
Alka

He was the senior who closed every deal, and I copied everything: "Let's park that thought," "Help me understand your pain point," even the way he leaned back with his hands behind his head. Diary, Thursday. Rajni.

Six weeks as a trainee at the newspaper and I've realised I've turned into a mini-Kunal. I say "Let's cut the fluff" in every meeting. I tap my pen twice before I speak, like he does. I even say "Right, right, right" when someone's talking. The funny thing is, it works. People listen more. I feel less like a kid pretending.

Today in the edit meeting I said "Let's cut the fluff" and my colleague Neha laughed and said, "Okay, Kunal." I laughed too, but it stung a bit.

So tonight I've been thinking. The pen-tap is useful; it makes me pause. "Cut the fluff" isn't really me; I like fluff. And "right, right, right" makes me sound like I'm not listening.

Tomorrow, I'll keep the pause. And try saying something in my own words.

qa.a: "Let's cut the fluff."

qa.a: Rajni felt embarrassed to realise how much of Kunal's style had been copied, and wondered what was really Rajni's own.

qa.a: Keeping the pen-tap pause that helps and dropping the phrases that don't fit is a way to test what truly suits, moving toward a personal style.
